steps.title: Overlapping groups
steps.intro: Two question types: a range (min and max) or an exact overlap.

tables.title: Range questions — the overlap
head: What
Rule
Example (\(12\) students: \(8\) and \(7\))
rows: \((A+B)-\text{total}\), or \(0\) if that is not positive

tables.title: Range questions — other regions (find the overlap range first)
head: Region
Rule
Example
rows: \(A+B-\text{both}\): from the larger group to \(A+B\) (at most the total)
\(\text{total}-\text{union}\): big when the union is small
\(A-\text{both}\): its minimum uses the MAXIMUM overlap

tips: "At most" / "at least" is about the thing they ask. Ask: to make THIS small, what must the overlap be?
Two shares adding to exactly the whole do NOT force an overlap; more than the whole does.
Percents? Stay in percent and change to people only at the end.
No total given? Look for a natural one: \(24\) hours, \(7\) days, \(100\%\). Awake \(18\) hours, at work \(10\) hours → both for at least \(18+10-24=4\) hours.
"Different items in either collection" is the union — neither is \(0\).

steps.stem: Of 45 campers, 28 bring a flashlight, 23 bring a map, and 16 bring both. How many bring neither?
explanation: Both is \(16\), therefore map only is \(23-16=7\).
At least one item: the whole flashlight group plus map only, \(28+7=35\).

steps.stem: A workshop has 22 machines. Of them, 14 cut, 12 polish, and 3 do neither. How many machines both cut and polish?
explanation: \(3\) machines do neither, therefore \(22-3=19\) do at least one job.
The two jobs add to \(14+12=26\). That is \(26-19=7\) more than \(19\). These \(7\) machines were counted twice, so \(7\) do both.

steps.stem: The people who both volunteer and study photography make up \(\frac16\) of the photography students and \(\frac14\) of all volunteers. What is the ratio of photography students who do not volunteer to volunteers who do not study photography?
explanation: Call the overlap \(x\). It is \(\frac16\) of the photography students, therefore there are \(6x\) photography students. It is \(\frac14\) of the volunteers, therefore there are \(4x\) volunteers.
Photography only: \(6x-x=5x\). Volunteers only: \(4x-x=3x\).
The ratio is \(5x:3x=5:3\). The group that does neither is not needed.

steps.stem: At a community event with 240 guests, 35% know the organizer and 80% know the host. What is the minimum number who know both?
explanation: \(35\%+80\%=115\%\), but the guests are only \(100\%\). So, at least \(115\%-100\%=15\%\) know both.
This minimum is possible: all \(20\%\) who do not know the host are in the organizer group, and the other \(35\%-20\%=15\%\) of the organizer group know the host.

steps.stem: A class has 48 students. Of them, 21 work in the greenhouse and 11 work in the orchard. Which of the following could be the number of students who work in neither place?
explanation: Neither \(=48-\text{union}\), where the union is everyone who works in at least one place.
Smallest union: all \(11\) orchard workers also work in the greenhouse, therefore the union is \(21\). Largest union: no overlap, \(21+11=32\) (less than \(48\), therefore it fits).
Neither goes from \(48-32=16\) to \(48-21=27\). Only \(18\) is in this range. It happens when the overlap is \(2\): the union is \(21+11-2=30\), and \(48-30=18\).

steps.stem: A club has 50 members. Of them, 32 swim and 27 run. At least how many members swim but do not run?
explanation: Swim but not run (swim only) \(=32-\text{both}\). It is smallest when "both" is largest.
Largest overlap: the smaller group — all \(27\) runners also swim. Then swim only is \(32-27=5\).
Check: \(27\) both, \(5\) swim only, \(0\) run only, and \(50-32=18\) do neither. Every number fits.
Trap: the minimum overlap \(32+27-50=9\) gives \(32-9=23\). That is the MOST swim only, not the least.

steps.stem: Of a company’s employees, \(\frac25\) can code, \(\frac45\) work remotely, \(\frac15\) are juniors, and \(\frac12\) are in training. Which statement is not necessarily true?
choices: At least one non-junior cannot code
At least one junior works remotely
At least one coder works remotely
At least one trainee cannot code
explanation: "At least one is in both groups" must be true only when the two groups add up to more than the whole.

Choice 1: non-juniors and non-coders, \(\frac45+\frac35=\frac75>1\) — forced. Choice 3: \(\frac25+\frac45=\frac65>1\) — forced. Choice 4: trainees and non-coders, \(\frac12+\frac35=\frac{11}{10}>1\) — forced.

Choice 2: juniors and remote workers, \(\frac15+\frac45=1\) exactly. This does not force an overlap. Out of \(10\) employees, the \(2\) juniors can work on site and the other \(8\) remotely. So, choice 2 is not necessarily true.

steps.stem: At lunch, \(\frac25\) of the staff choose soup, \(\frac14\) choose salad, and \(\frac1{10}\) choose both. Exactly 8 people choose both. How many choose neither?
explanation: \(\frac1{10}\) of the staff is \(8\) people, therefore the staff is \(8\cdot10=80\).
Soup: \(\frac25\cdot80=32\). Salad: \(\frac14\cdot80=20\). At least one: \(32+20-8=44\).

steps.stem: Two researchers photograph butterflies. One photographs 31 butterflies and the other photographs 22. Together, their photographs show 40 different butterflies. How many butterflies appear in both collections?
explanation: The \(40\) butterflies are the ones in at least one collection (the union), therefore neither is \(0\).
The first researcher has \(31\) of the \(40\). The other \(40-31=9\) appear only in the second collection.

steps.stem: In a school, \(40\%\) of the students are in the upper grades and the rest are in the lower grades. \(30\%\) of the upper-grade students and \(60\%\) of the lower-grade students walk to school. What percent of the students who walk to school are in the upper grades?
explanation: Plug in \(100\) students: \(40\) in the upper grades and \(60\) in the lower grades.
Upper grades who walk: \(30\%\) of \(40\) is \(12\). Lower grades who walk: \(60\%\) of \(60\) is \(36\). Walkers: \(12+36=48\).
"Of the students who walk" means the whole is \(48\): \(\frac{12}{48}=\frac14=25\%\).

steps.stem: In a survey, \(80\%\) of the people own a phone, \(75\%\) own a laptop, and \(70\%\) own a tablet. At least what percent of the people own all three?
explanation: Plug in \(100\) people. No phone: \(20\). No laptop: \(25\). No tablet: \(30\).
At most \(20+25+30=75\) people miss at least one item. So, at least \(100-75=25\) own all three: \(25\%\).
Traps: \(55\%\) uses only two groups (\(80+75-100\)), and \(70\%\) is the maximum (the smallest group).

steps.title: Two-way tables and three groups
steps.intro: Two traits of the same people → a table. Three groups → count who is missing.

tables.title: Three groups
head: What
Rule
Example
rows: total \(-\) (missing A \(+\) missing B \(+\) missing C), or \(0\)
Max in all three, pairs given

tips: Percents in a table? Plug in \(100\).
"Of the …" tells you the whole: that row or that column.
Rows add across, columns add down.

steps.stem: Every one of a group of students studies art, music, or both. There are 26 art students, 19 music students, and 11 who study both. How many students are in the group?
explanation: Adding \(26\) and \(19\) counts the \(11\) students who study both twice. Remove one copy: \(26+19-11=34\).
Or split into separate groups: art only \(26-11=15\), music only \(19-11=8\), both \(11\). Total: \(15+8+11=34\).

steps.stem: Of 150 employees, 90 work remotely at least once a week, 75 work flexibly, and 60 do both. How many do exactly one of these?
explanation: Remote only: \(90-60=30\). Flexible only: \(75-60=15\).
Exactly one: \(30+15=45\). In one line: \(90+75-2\cdot60=45\).

steps.stem: A school has 80 pupils: 50 study French, 40 study German, and 25 study both. Of the pupils who study French, what fraction also study German?
explanation: "Of the pupils who study French" means the whole is the \(50\) French pupils.
\(25\) of them also study German: \(\frac{25}{50}=\frac12\).

steps.stem: Of 120 hikers, 54 carry a map, 82 carry a compass, and 31 carry both. How many carry neither?
explanation: At least one item: \(54+82-31=105\).

steps.stem: Among 64 visitors, 39 enter the gallery, 31 enter the garden, and 12 enter neither. How many enter exactly one of the two places?
explanation: Exactly one \(=\text{union}-\text{both}=52-18=34\).

steps.stem: A class has 30 students, and 18 of them are girls. 12 students wear glasses, and 5 of those are boys. How many girls do not wear glasses?
explanation: Girls who wear glasses: \(12-5=7\).
Girls who do not wear glasses: \(18-7=11\).

steps.stem: A class has 48 students. Of them, 28 swim and 24 cycle. Three quarters of the cyclists also swim. How many students do neither activity?
explanation: Both: \(\frac34\cdot24=18\).

steps.stem: At a fair, 150 different people each win one prize. Of the winners, 65% live nearby and 55% arrived by train. What is the minimum number who both live nearby and arrived by train?
explanation: \(65\%+55\%=120\%\) of the winners, but there are only \(100\%\). So, at least \(120\%-100\%=20\%\) are in both groups.

steps.stem: Every member of a club speaks Spanish, Italian, or both. Spanish speakers are \(\frac34\) of the club and Italian speakers are \(\frac58\). What fraction speaks both?
explanation: Everyone is in at least one group, therefore neither is \(0\).
Both: \(\frac34+\frac58-1=\frac68+\frac58-\frac88=\frac38\).

steps.stem: A survey of 90 people finds that 48 use buses and 57 use trains. What is the range of possible numbers of people who use both?
explanation: Maximum: the smaller group, \(48\) (all bus users also use trains).
So, the number is from \(15\) to \(48\).

steps.stem: In a team, 55% can code and 45% can design. Twenty percent do neither. What percentage can do both?
explanation: \(20\%\) do neither, therefore \(100\%-20\%=80\%\) do at least one.
Note: \(55\%+45\%=100\%\) alone does not force an overlap. The extra fact "\(20\%\) do neither" is what forces it.

steps.stem: Of 40 workers, 18 speak Arabic and 15 speak Russian. Which of the following could be the number of workers who speak at least one of these two languages?
explanation: At least one \(=18+15-\text{both}=33-\text{both}\).
Largest overlap \(15\): at least one is \(18\) (the larger group). No overlap: at least one is \(33\) (less than \(40\), therefore it fits).
So, the number is from \(18\) to \(33\). Only \(30\) is in this range (overlap \(3\)).

steps.stem: Of 80 guests, 50 drink coffee and 45 drink tea. What is the greatest possible number of guests who drink neither?
explanation: Neither \(=80-\text{union}\). It is greatest when the union is smallest.
The smallest union is the larger group, \(50\): all \(45\) tea drinkers also drink coffee.
Neither: \(80-50=30\). (Using the smaller group, \(80-45=35\), is a trap: the \(50\) coffee drinkers are never in neither.)

steps.stem: A bag contains 72 badges: 48 are round and 30 are metal. At least how many round badges are not metal?
explanation: Round but not metal \(=48-\text{both}\). It is smallest when "both" is largest.
Largest overlap: all \(30\) metal badges are round. Then \(48-30=18\) round badges are not metal.

steps.stem: A firm gives one company tablet to each of \(\frac35\) of its employees, using 72 tablets. Half of all employees also own a personal tablet. What is the minimum number with both a company and a personal tablet?
explanation: \(\frac35\) of the employees is \(72\), therefore \(\frac15\) is \(72\div3=24\) and the total is \(24\cdot5=120\).
Personal tablets: \(\frac12\cdot120=60\).
Minimum overlap: \(72+60-120=12\).

steps.stem: Each of 60 trainees gets a score from 0 to 12. Of them, 26 score from 9 to 12, 24 score from 7 to 10, and 20 score below 7. How many trainees score from 9 to 10? (All ranges include both ends.)
explanation: Together, the bands "9 to 12" and "7 to 10" cover every score from 7 to 12. Everyone who does not score below 7 is in at least one band: \(60-20=40\).
The two bands share the scores 9 to 10. That is the overlap: \(26+24-40=10\).

steps.stem: Of 250 students, 205 enjoy chess and 190 play a musical instrument. What is the greatest possible percentage who neither enjoy chess nor play an instrument?
explanation: Neither \(=250-\text{union}\). Neither is greatest when the union is smallest.
The union is at least the larger group, \(205\). It is exactly \(205\) when all \(190\) musicians also enjoy chess.

steps.stem: Of a shop’s bags, \(\frac23\) are blue, \(\frac34\) have zips, and \(\frac12\) are both blue and zipped. What is the ratio of blue bags without zips to zipped bags that are not blue?
explanation: Blue without zips: \(\frac23-\frac12=\frac16\). Zipped but not blue: \(\frac34-\frac12=\frac14\).
The ratio is \(\frac16:\frac14\). Multiply both parts by \(12\): the ratio is \(2:3\).

steps.stem: At a factory, \(70\%\) of the workers work the day shift and the rest work the night shift. \(10\%\) of the day-shift workers and \(40\%\) of the night-shift workers are new. What percent of all the workers are new?
explanation: Plug in \(100\) workers: \(70\) day shift and \(30\) night shift.
The average of \(10\%\) and \(40\%\) (\(25\%\)) is wrong: the two percents are of groups of different sizes.

steps.stem: A club has 90 members. Of them, 60 play tennis and 45 play golf. What is the greatest possible number of members who play tennis but not golf?
explanation: Tennis only \(=60-\text{both}\). It is greatest when "both" is smallest.
Smallest overlap: \(60+45-90=15\).
Tennis only: \(60-15=45\). (\(60\) is impossible: at least \(15\) tennis players also play golf.)

steps.stem: In a town, \(\frac35\) of residents cycle, \(\frac14\) grow vegetables, \(\frac25\) keep pets, and \(\frac45\) are under 50. Which of the following overlaps necessarily contains at least one resident?
choices: Residents aged at least 50 who grow vegetables
explanation: Two groups must overlap only when they add up to more than the whole.
Under 50 and pet owners: \(\frac45+\frac25=\frac65>1\) — forced.

The others: cyclists and vegetable growers, \(\frac35+\frac14=\frac{17}{20}<1\). Aged at least 50 and vegetable growers, \(\frac15+\frac14=\frac{9}{20}<1\). Cyclists and pet owners, \(\frac35+\frac25=1\) — not more than \(1\). These groups can be separate.

steps.stem: Of 60 students, 42 take chemistry and 35 take biology. What is the greatest possible number of students who take exactly one of these two subjects?
explanation: Exactly one \(=42+35-2\cdot\text{both}=77-2\cdot\text{both}\). It is greatest when "both" is smallest.
Smallest overlap: \(42+35-60=17\).
Exactly one: \(77-2\cdot17=77-34=43\). (With the largest overlap, \(35\), exactly one is only \(77-70=7\).)

steps.stem: In a group, \(\frac35\) of the people are adults and the rest are children. \(\frac14\) of the adults and \(\frac12\) of the children play chess. What fraction of the chess players are children?
explanation: Plug in \(20\) people: \(12\) adults and \(8\) children.
Chess players: \(\frac14\cdot12=3\) adults and \(\frac12\cdot8=4\) children, \(7\) in all.
"Of the chess players" means the whole is \(7\): \(\frac47\) are children.

steps.stem: Of 60 students, 45 study math, 40 study art, and 50 study music. What is the smallest possible number of students who study all three?
explanation: Count who misses a subject: no math \(60-45=15\), no art \(60-40=20\), no music \(60-50=10\).
At most \(15+20+10=45\) students miss a subject. So, at least \(60-45=15\) study all three.

steps.stem: In a group of 100 readers, 70 read fiction, 65 read history, and 60 read science. What is the minimum possible number who read all three?
explanation: Count who misses a group: no fiction \(100-70=30\), no history \(100-65=35\), no science \(100-60=40\).
\(30+35+40=105\) — more than the \(100\) readers. So, no one is forced into all three (\(70+65+60-2\cdot100=-5\) is negative), and the minimum can be \(0\).

Check that \(0\) really works: \(35\) read fiction and history, \(30\) read fiction and science, \(30\) read history and science, and \(5\) read fiction only. Fiction: \(35+30+5=70\). History: \(35+30=65\). Science: \(30+30=60\). Total: \(35+30+30+5=100\), and nobody reads all three.

steps.stem: In a school, 50 students sing in the choir, 45 play in the band, and 40 are in the drama club. 14 students are in both the choir and the band, 11 are in both the choir and the drama club, and 16 are in both the band and the drama club. What is the greatest possible number of students who are in all three?
explanation: A student in all three is also in each of the three pairs. Therefore the number in all three is at most the smallest pair overlap: \(11\).

\(11\) is possible: put the \(11\) choir and drama students in the band too. Then choir and band only \(=14-11=3\), band and drama only \(=16-11=5\). Every group has room: choir \(11+3=14\le50\), band \(11+3+5=19\le45\), drama \(11+5=16\le40\).
Traps: \(40\) is the smallest group (the ceiling only when the pairs are not given), \(16\) is the largest pair, and \(41=14+11+16\) adds the pairs.
